column9: How much energy from the cell does **passive transport** use?
column14: A small amount of ATP from the mitochondria
column15: A large amount of ATP, more than active transport
column16: Energy from sunlight captured by chloroplasts
column17: None; it requires no energy from the cell
column28: Passive transport moves substances across the membrane without using the cell's energy. Molecules move on their own from high to low concentration. Active transport is the kind that uses ATP.
column29: Think about which direction molecules move in passive transport. Do they need a push to go that way?

column9: In diffusion, molecules move from ___.
column14: an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration
column15: an area of low concentration to an area of high concentration
column16: an area of high concentration to low, but only when the cell spends ATP
column17: the outside of the cell to the inside, no matter where the concentration is higher
column28: Diffusion moves molecules from HIGH to LOW concentration, down the concentration gradient, with no energy. It never needs ATP, and it goes whichever way the gradient points, in or out of the cell. Moving from low to high takes energy (active transport).
column29: Think of the air freshener demo: where does the smell spread?

column9: Osmosis is the diffusion of ___ across a membrane.
column28: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane. Diffusion can involve any molecule; osmosis is only water.
column29: Think of the osmosis lab: the dialysis bags gained or lost mass. Which substance was crossing the membrane?

column9: Active transport requires energy in the form of ATP.
column28: True. Active transport uses ATP to move molecules from low to high concentration, against the concentration gradient.
column29: Active means doing work. What is the cell's energy molecule?

column9: What makes up the main structure of the cell membrane?
column14: A single stiff layer of cellulose fibers, like wood
column15: Two layers of phospholipids (a phospholipid bilayer)
column16: A thick protective wall made of DNA
column17: Two layers of starch (a starch bilayer)
column28: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with proteins and cholesterol embedded in it. Cellulose makes plant cell walls.
column29: Picture the membrane drawing in your notes: how many layers are there, and what molecule makes up each layer?

column9: Because the cell membrane lets some substances pass through but not others, it is called selectively ___.
column28: The membrane is selectively permeable (semi-permeable): small, uncharged molecules pass through easily, but large molecules and ions need help.
column29: It is the word for "able to be passed through."

column9: Which of these are types of passive transport? Select all that apply.
column14: Facilitated diffusion
column15: Exocytosis
column16: Osmosis
column17: Sodium-potassium pump
column28: The three types of passive transport are diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and osmosis; none of them use energy. The sodium-potassium pump, endocytosis, and exocytosis all use ATP, so they are active transport.
column29: For each one, ask: does the cell have to spend energy to make it happen? If not, it is passive.

column9: The cell membrane is essential for homeostasis. What does **homeostasis** mean?
column14: Moving water out of the cell
column15: Making proteins for the cell
column16: Maintaining an internal balance
column17: Splitting into two brand-new cells
column28: Homeostasis means maintaining an internal balance (stable conditions inside). The membrane helps by controlling what enters and leaves.
column29: Think of the thermostat in your house. What is its job?

column9: Phagocytosis, or "cell eating," is when a cell wraps its membrane around a large particle and pulls it inside. Phagocytosis is a type of ___.
column14: endocytosis
column15: exocytosis
column16: osmosis
column17: facilitated diffusion
column28: Endocytosis brings large materials INTO the cell by folding the membrane around them to form a vesicle; phagocytosis is the cell-eating kind. Exocytosis moves materials out, and osmosis and facilitated diffusion are passive.
column29: Endo- means in; exo- means out.

column9: When a cell membrane separates two solutions, water moves toward the side that has more solute.
column28: True. More solute means less water, so water moves from the side with less solute (more water) to the side with more solute (less water).
column29: Water moves from where there is more water to where there is less water.

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Solute :: The substance that gets dissolved
column15: Solvent :: The substance that does the dissolving
column16: Solution :: A mixture with a solute evenly spread through a liquid
column17: Concentration gradient :: A difference in concentration between two areas
column18: Equilibrium :: Equal concentration everywhere; molecules still move but there is no net change
column28: Solute = what dissolves. Solvent = what does the dissolving. Solution = the even mixture you end up with. Concentration gradient = a difference in concentration between two areas. Equilibrium = evenly spread; molecules keep moving, but there is no net change.
column29: Think of making a drink from a powder: what dissolves, what does the dissolving, and the mixture you end up with.

column9: Facilitated diffusion uses ATP, because transport proteins are involved.
column28: False. Facilitated diffusion is passive: it uses no energy. Molecules still move from high to low concentration; the channel or carrier protein just gives them a way through.
column29: "Facilitate" means to help. Is it passive or active?

column9: Which substance can cross the cell membrane easily on its own?
column14: A large protein
column15: Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
column16: A sodium ion (Na⁺)
column17: A starch molecule
column28: Small molecules like H₂O, CO₂, and O₂ move through the membrane easily. Large molecules (proteins, starch) and ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻) can't cross on their own.
column29: Which choice is a small, uncharged molecule?

column9: A cell is 92% water. If the rest of the cell is solute, what percent of the cell is solute?
column28: Water and solute together make up 100% of the cell, so 100% − 92% water = 8% solute. Finding the percent solute like this is the first step when you compare a cell to a solution to decide if the solution is hypertonic, hypotonic, or isotonic.
column29: Water + solute = 100% of the cell.

column9: In a glass of Kool-Aid, which part is the **solvent**?
column14: The sugar
column15: The drink mix powder
column16: The water
column17: The ice cubes
column28: The solvent does the dissolving; in Kool-Aid that is water. The sugar and drink mix are the solutes.
column29: Which part does the dissolving?

column9: A cell has a sugar concentration of 10%. The solution around it has a sugar concentration of 20%. What term describes the solution?
column14: Hypotonic
column15: Isotonic
column16: Equilibrium
column17: Hypertonic
column28: The solution has MORE solute (20%) than the cell (10%), so the solution is hypertonic. Water will move out of the cell toward the higher solute.
column29: Hyper- means more. Does the outside have more or less solute than the cell?

column9: A cell is 2% salt inside. It is placed in a solution that is 0.5% salt. Which way will water move?
column14: Into the cell, from the solution
column15: Out of the cell, into the solution
column16: It depends on whether it is a plant or animal cell
column17: Salt moves out of the cell instead of water
column28: The cell has more salt (less water) than the solution, so water moves from the solution (more water) into the cell. The solution is hypotonic. Water moves the same way in plant and animal cells, because only the solute difference decides the direction. In osmosis it is the water that moves across the membrane, not the salt.
column29: Water moves toward the side with MORE solute.

column9: What happens to water when a cell is placed in an **isotonic** solution?
column14: More water moves into the cell than out, so the cell swells.
column15: Water moves in and out equally, so there is no net movement.
column16: More water moves out of the cell than in, so the cell shrinks.
column17: Water stops crossing the membrane because the two sides are balanced.
column28: Isotonic means the solute concentration is the same inside and out. Water still crosses the membrane (it never stops), but equal amounts enter and leave, so there is no net movement and the cell stays the same size. Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, and shrinking in a hypertonic one.
column29: Iso- means equal. Remember what your notes say molecules are doing at equilibrium.

column9: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water (pure water). What will happen to it?
column14: It will shrink and shrivel.
column15: It will swell and burst.
column16: It will stay exactly the same.
column17: It will swell a little, then stop.
column28: Pure water is hypotonic compared to the cell, so water rushes in. An animal cell has no cell wall, so it keeps swelling until it bursts; it does not stop partway. Shrinking would need water to leave the cell, and the cell can't stay the same because water is moving in.
column29: Pure water has no solute. Which way will water move, and what holds an animal cell together?

column9: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What will happen to it?
column14: Water leaves and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
column15: Water enters and the cell gets firm; the wall keeps it from bursting.
column16: Water enters until the cell swells up and bursts open.
column17: Water leaves the cell because its vacuole is already full.
column28: Pure water is hypotonic, so water moves in and the large vacuole swells. The cell wall pushes back (turgor pressure), so the cell gets firm instead of bursting. That is why watered plants stand up straight. Water does not leave the cell, even when the vacuole is full, because the cell still has more solute than the pure water around it.
column29: Water moves in. What does a plant cell have that an animal cell doesn't?

column9: A red blood cell is about 0.9% salt inside. Put these solutions in order from the one that makes the cell GAIN the most water to the one that makes it LOSE the most water.
column14: 0.3% salt
column15: 0.9% salt
column16: 10% salt
column17: Distilled water (0% salt)
column28: The less salt outside, the more water rushes in, so distilled water causes the biggest gain. 0.9% matches the cell (isotonic, no net change). Above 0.9%, the solution is hypertonic, and 10% pulls out the most water.
column29: Compare each solution to the cell's 0.9%. Less salt outside means water moves in.

column9: In facilitated diffusion, ___ proteins change shape to move a molecule from one side of the membrane to the other.
column28: Carrier proteins change shape to carry material across. Channel proteins are different: they have a pore that materials pass through.
column29: It is not the kind of transport protein with an open pore (a channel). What is the other kind called in your notes?

column9: In the food coloring demo, the color spread much faster in hot water than in cold water. Why?
column14: Hot water has less water in it.
column15: Molecules move faster at higher temperatures.
column16: Food coloring needs energy from heat to stay mixed.
column17: Heat shrinks the dye molecules, so they spread faster.
column28: Temperature is one of the factors that affects the rate of diffusion. Hot water molecules move faster and bump the dye around faster, so it spreads faster. The dye molecules stay the same size in hot water; they just move faster. Hot water is still all water, and the dye doesn't need heat energy to stay mixed.
column29: What does heat do to how fast molecules move?

column9: In a nerve cell, the Na⁺ concentration is about 15 mmol/L inside the cell and about 145 mmol/L outside it. The cell keeps moving Na⁺ from the inside to the outside. Which statement describes this movement?
column14: Down its gradient (high to low), so no energy is needed
column15: Down its gradient (high to low), but it still uses ATP
column16: Against its gradient (low to high), but no energy is needed
column17: Against its gradient (low to high), so the cell uses ATP
column28: Na⁺ is moving from inside (about 15) to outside (about 145), so it goes from low to high concentration, against its gradient. That takes energy, so the cell has to spend ATP. This is active transport by the sodium-potassium pump, which is critical for sending nerve impulses. The ions are not moving down their gradient (high to low), which is the passive, no-energy direction, and nothing can move against its gradient without energy.
column29: Compare the two numbers. Is Na⁺ going from the side with more to the side with less, or the other way?

column9: Which of these require the cell to use energy (ATP)? Select all that apply.
column14: An amoeba wraps its membrane around a smaller organism and pulls it inside.
column15: Oxygen moves from the blood into a muscle cell that has less oxygen.
column16: Moving glucose into a cell that already has more glucose inside than outside.
column17: A stomach cell moves H⁺ ions into the stomach, where H⁺ is already far more concentrated.
column18: Water moves into a root cell from wet soil.
column19: Potassium ions leak out of a nerve cell through an open channel, from high to low.
column28: Moving glucose and H⁺ ions from low to high concentration goes against the gradient, so those need ATP (active transport). Wrapping the membrane around a whole organism is endocytosis, which also uses ATP. Oxygen diffusing into the muscle cell, water entering the root cell by osmosis, and K⁺ leaking out through an open channel all go from high to low, so they are passive, even when a protein helps.
column29: For each one, ask: could this happen on its own, just by molecules spreading from high to low concentration?

column9: Match each form of transport to its description.
column14: Diffusion :: Molecules move from high to low concentration through the bilayer
column15: Facilitated diffusion :: Molecules move from high to low through a transport protein
column16: Sodium-potassium pump :: Uses ATP to move ions from low to high concentration
column17: Endocytosis :: The membrane folds in to bring large particles inside
column18: Exocytosis :: A vesicle fuses with the membrane to release materials outside
column28: Diffusion: high to low, no help. Facilitated diffusion: high to low through a protein. Pump: ATP, low to high. Endocytosis: in by folding the membrane. Exocytosis: out by a vesicle fusing.
column29: Sort into passive (no energy) and active (energy) first.

column9: When an animal cell swells with water until it bursts, the bursting is called ___.
column28: In a hypotonic solution, water rushes into an animal cell, and with no cell wall it bursts. This is cytolysis. In a hypertonic solution an animal cell shrinks instead; in a plant cell the membrane pulls away from the cell wall, and that is plasmolysis.
column29: In your notes this word is paired with plasmolysis (the plant-cell word). It names what happens to an animal cell in a hypotonic solution.

column9: Which situation is an example of **facilitated diffusion**?
column14: Oxygen slips through the bilayer from the lungs into the blood.
column15: A nerve cell uses ATP to pump sodium ions out of the cell.
column16: Glucose enters a red blood cell through a carrier protein, high to low.
column17: A white blood cell wraps its membrane around a bacterium and pulls it in.
column28: Facilitated diffusion needs a transport protein but no energy, and it goes from high to low. Oxygen crosses the bilayer by simple diffusion, the pump uses ATP, and engulfing is endocytosis.
column29: Look for a protein helping, with no energy used.

column9: A 47-inch muskie from Lake Wissota (fresh water) is moved into the Atlantic Ocean (salt water). How would you describe the ocean compared to the muskie's cells?
column14: Hypotonic, so its cells would gain water
column15: Isotonic, so nothing would change
column16: Hypertonic, so its cells would gain water
column17: Hypertonic, so its cells would lose water
column28: Ocean water has much more salt than a freshwater fish's cells, so it is hypertonic. Water moves out of the cells toward the higher solute, and the cells shrink. The cells don't gain water: in a hypertonic solution, water leaves. Hypotonic would mean the ocean had less solute than the cells.
column29: Which has more solute: the ocean or the fish's cells?

column9: In the osmosis lab, a dialysis bag of sucrose solution had an initial mass of 12.0 g. After soaking in distilled water, its final mass was 13.8 g. What was the percent change in mass? (% change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100)
column28: % change = (13.8 g − 12.0 g) ÷ 12.0 g × 100 = 1.8 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 15%. The bag gained mass because water moved into it by osmosis.
column29: Subtract initial from final first, then divide by the INITIAL mass and multiply by 100.

column9: Joseph's mom sprinkles sugar over cut fruit and leaves the bowl in the fridge overnight. In the morning, the fruit is sitting in liquid. Where did the liquid come from?
column14: Water moved out of the fruit cells by osmosis toward the sugar.
column15: The sugar melted into a liquid in the fridge.
column16: Water moved into the fruit cells by active transport.
column17: The cold air in the fridge added extra moisture to the fruit bowl.
column28: The sugar made a hypertonic coating around the fruit, so water left the fruit cells by osmosis and collected in the bowl. Sugar doesn't melt in a fridge, and osmosis is passive.
column29: The sugar outside is a high solute concentration. Which way does water move?

column9: Why do grocery stores sprinkle fresh vegetables with water?
column14: The water washes away the vegetables' tough cell walls.
column15: Water moves out of the cells, making the vegetables lighter to sell.
column16: Water enters the cells by osmosis, keeping them firm and crisp.
column17: The vegetables use the water to power active transport.
column28: Plain water is hypotonic to the plant cells, so water moves in, the vacuoles fill, and turgor pressure against the cell wall keeps the vegetables crisp. Without it, they lose water and wilt.
column29: Is plain water hypotonic or hypertonic to plant cells?

column9: In the diffusion lab, a dialysis bag holds glucose and starch, and the beaker holds water and Lugol's iodine (IKI). After 30 minutes the solution inside the bag turns blue-black. What happened?
column14: IKI moved into the bag and reacted with the starch.
column15: Starch moved out of the bag into the beaker.
column16: Glucose turned into starch inside the bag.
column17: Water moved out of the bag and left the color behind.
column28: Iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch. The color change happened INSIDE the bag, so the iodine (IKI) must have diffused in through the membrane's pores. Starch leaving the bag would not explain a color change inside it, glucose does not turn into starch, and water leaving cannot create a new color.
column29: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Where did the color change happen?

column9: Calcium ions are much more concentrated outside a muscle cell than inside it. When a calcium channel protein opens, calcium ions will flow OUT of the cell through it.
column28: False. A channel protein is passive (facilitated diffusion), so ions can only flow through it from high to low concentration. Calcium is more concentrated outside, so it flows IN. Moving calcium out, against its gradient, would take a pump and ATP.
column29: Does a channel protein use energy? Then which way can ions move through it?

column9: Why can't sodium (Na⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻) ions cross the cell membrane on their own?
column14: They are too large to fit between the phospholipids.
column15: They are charged, so they need proteins to get through the bilayer.
column16: They are hydrophobic, so the water inside the cell pushes them away.
column17: The membrane only lets water molecules through, and nothing else.
column28: Ions are charged (hydrophilic), so they can't pass through the lipid tails in the middle of the bilayer on their own. They cross through transport proteins (facilitated diffusion) or pumps (active transport). Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are very small, so size isn't the problem; they are hydrophilic, not hydrophobic; and the membrane lets other small molecules like CO₂ and O₂ through too.
column29: The middle of the bilayer is made of lipid tails. Do charged particles mix with lipids?

column9: A jellyfish from the ocean is placed in Lake Superior (fresh water). What would happen to its cells?
column14: Water would rush into its cells, and they would swell and could burst.
column15: Water would leave its cells, and they would shrink.
column16: Its cells would stay the same size, since both are natural water.
column17: Salt would rush into its cells by active transport.
column28: Ocean animals' cells are salty. Fresh lake water has far less solute, so it is hypotonic to them. Water moves in by osmosis, and cells with no cell wall swell and can burst. Lake water does not match ocean animals' cells just because both are natural water; it has much less salt. Water would not leave the cells, because the lake has less salt than they do, and salt does not rush in by active transport.
column29: Compare the salt in a jellyfish's cells to the salt in Lake Superior.

column9: Normal I.V. saline is 0.9% salt, about the same as the inside of red blood cells. A nurse almost hangs a bag of 5% saline by mistake. What would the 5% bag do to the patient's red blood cells?
column14: It is hypotonic, so water would rush in and they would burst.
column15: It is isotonic, so nothing would change.
column16: It is hypertonic, so water would leave them and they would shrink.
column17: It is hypertonic, so salt would rush in and make them burst.
column28: 5% salt is more than the 0.9% inside the cells, so the bag is hypertonic to them. More water would leave the red blood cells than enter, so they would shrink and shrivel. Salt does not rush in to burst them; bursting happens in a hypotonic solution, and an isotonic bag would match the cells.
column29: Compare the 5% bag to the inside of the cells. Which way will water move?

column9: Roads are salted to melt ice in the winter. In the spring, many plants along the roadside wilt and die. What is the best explanation?
column14: The salt is hypotonic, so the root cells burst.
column15: The salt on the ground blocks sunlight from reaching the plants' leaves.
column16: Salty soil is hypertonic, so water leaves the root cells by osmosis.
column17: The root cells use active transport to pump in too much water.
column28: Salt in the soil raises the solute concentration outside the roots, making it hypertonic. Water leaves the root cells instead of entering, the cells undergo plasmolysis, and the plant wilts.
column29: Which has more solute now: the salty soil or the root cells?

column9: A person stranded on a raft drinks ocean water. Why does this make dehydration worse?
column14: Salt pulls water into the cells by active transport.
column15: The cells use ATP to pump their own water out.
column16: The cells stop letting water in until the salt is gone.
column17: Water leaves the cells by osmosis toward the saltier side.
column28: Ocean water is saltier than body cells, so it is hypertonic to them. Water moves out of the cells by osmosis toward the higher salt, leaving the person even more dehydrated. Osmosis is passive, so no ATP is spent: salt does not pull water in by active transport, and the cells do not pump their water out. Water doesn't stop crossing the membrane either; more of it simply leaves than enters.
column29: Where will the salt end up, and which way will water move?

column9: In the diffusion lab, a dialysis bag holding glucose and starch sits in a beaker of water and Lugol's iodine (IKI). After 30 minutes, a glucose test strip shows glucose in the beaker water, but the beaker water never turns blue-black. What does this tell you?
column14: Starch fits through the bag's pores, but glucose is too large.
column15: Both glucose and starch fit through the bag's pores.
column16: Glucose fits through the bag's pores, but starch is too large.
column17: The dialysis tubing uses ATP to pump the glucose out.
column28: Glucose left the bag, so it fits through the pores. If starch had left, the iodine in the beaker would have turned blue-black, so starch stayed inside. The membrane sorts molecules by size, with no energy needed. Starch is the larger molecule, so it is not the one that got through, and dialysis tubing is not alive, so it can't use ATP.
column29: Which molecule was found outside the bag, and which molecule would have turned the beaker blue-black?

column9: A potato core with a mass of 4.0 g is soaked in salt water for 30 minutes. Its final mass is 3.6 g. What is its percent change in mass? Use a negative number for a loss.
column28: % change = (3.6 g − 4.0 g) ÷ 4.0 g × 100 = −0.4 ÷ 4.0 × 100 = −10%. The core lost water because the salt water was hypertonic.
column29: Final minus initial will be negative here. Then divide by the initial mass and multiply by 100.

column9: Potato cores were soaked in salt solutions. Data table: Salt (mol/L): 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 | % change in mass: +8, +3, −1, −4, −9. Between which two salt concentrations would a solution be isotonic to the potato cells?
column14: Between 0.0 and 0.1 mol/L
column15: Between 0.1 and 0.2 mol/L
column16: Between 0.2 and 0.3 mol/L
column17: Between 0.3 and 0.4 mol/L
column28: An isotonic solution causes no net water movement, so the % change in mass would be 0. The cores gained mass at 0.1 mol/L (+3%, hypotonic) and lost mass at 0.2 mol/L (−1%, hypertonic), so the zero point lies between 0.1 and 0.2 mol/L. The −1% at 0.2 is close to zero, but it is still a loss, so 0.2 and 0.3 are both hypertonic; 0.0 and 0.1 are both gains, and 0.3 and 0.4 are both losses.
column29: What % change in mass would an isotonic solution cause? Find where the data would hit that number.

column9: A poison stops a cell from making ATP. Which forms of transport would stop?
column14: Facilitated diffusion and active transport would stop, since both use proteins.
column15: Diffusion and osmosis would stop, but active transport would continue.
column16: Pumps would stop, but endocytosis and exocytosis would continue.
column17: Active transport would stop, but diffusion and osmosis would continue.
column28: Only active transport uses ATP, and that includes pumps AND vesicle transport (endocytosis, exocytosis), so all of those would stop. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and osmosis are passive; they are driven by the concentration gradient, so they keep going. Facilitated diffusion uses proteins but no energy.
column29: Which forms of transport need ATP in the first place?

column9: A plant's root cells keep absorbing minerals from the soil even though the minerals are already MORE concentrated inside the cells. What type of transport is this?
column14: Active transport
column15: Simple diffusion
column16: Osmosis
column17: Facilitated diffusion
column28: Moving minerals from low (soil) to high (root cell) concentration goes against the gradient, so it must be active transport using ATP. Every passive process moves from high to low.
column29: Which direction are the minerals moving compared to the gradient?

column9: A nerve cell packs signal molecules into vesicles. The vesicles fuse with the cell membrane and release the molecules outside the cell. How should this be classified?
column14: Exocytosis, a form of passive transport
column15: Endocytosis, a form of active transport
column16: Facilitated diffusion, a form of passive transport
column17: Exocytosis, a form of active transport
column28: Vesicles fusing with the membrane to release materials OUT of the cell is exocytosis, and moving vesicles takes energy, so it is active transport. Exocytosis is never passive, endocytosis brings materials in, and facilitated diffusion moves molecules through transport proteins, not vesicles.
column29: Is the material going in or out, and does moving vesicles take energy?

column9: A 6-year-old carves two boats out of a potato and floats both in the sink. He puts salt inside one boat as cargo and leaves the other empty. Nobody touches either boat. An hour later, the salted boat has water inside it, but the empty boat is still dry. Which explanation is correct?
column14: The salt pulled water into the boat by active transport.
column15: The salt dissolved and leaked out of the boat into the sink water.
column16: Water moved by osmosis through the potato toward the salty side.
column17: Water soaked through the potato like a sponge; the salt did not matter.
column28: The salt inside the boat made a high solute concentration, so water moved by osmosis out of the potato's cells (and from the sink water beyond them) toward the salt. The empty boat is the control: it stayed dry, so the potato does not just soak up water like a sponge; the salt made the difference. Osmosis is passive, not active transport, and salt leaking out would not put water into the boat.
column29: Compare the two boats. What was different about the one that filled with water?

column9: Three dialysis bags each start at 10.0 g and sit in pure water. Bag A holds pure water, Bag B 10% sucrose solution, and Bag C 30% sucrose solution. After 30 minutes: A = 10.0 g, B = 11.5 g, C = 13.5 g. Why did Bag C gain the most mass?
column14: Its concentration gradient was biggest, so the most water moved in.
column15: Sucrose moved out of Bag C and was replaced by heavier water.
column16: Bag C used the most ATP to actively pump water in through its pores.
column17: Bag C was the control group, so it changed the most.
column28: The bigger the concentration gradient, the more water moves in by osmosis. Bag C had the most solute (30% sucrose), so it gained the most. The sucrose stays inside the bags; the extra mass is water moving in. Bag A is the control (no gradient, no change), and osmosis doesn't use ATP.
column29: Compare the concentration gradient between each bag and the pure water.

column9: Which changes would make diffusion happen FASTER? Select all that apply.
column14: Lowering the temperature
column15: Making both sides the same concentration
column16: Making the concentration difference larger
column17: Raising the temperature
column28: Diffusion speeds up when molecules move faster (higher temperature), when the gradient is steeper (bigger difference), and when the molecules are smaller. Equal concentrations mean equilibrium: no net diffusion at all.
column29: The notes list temperature and size of molecules. What else makes molecules spread faster?

column9: A plant cell in a hypertonic solution does not lose any water, because its cell wall stops water from leaving.
column28: False. The cell wall is not a barrier to water. In a hypertonic solution water leaves the vacuole and cytoplasm, and the cell membrane shrinks away from the wall (plasmolysis), so the plant wilts. The wall only keeps a plant cell from bursting in a hypotonic solution.
column29: Does the cell wall control what goes in and out, or just give support?

column9: Put the steps in order to show how a white blood cell takes in a bacterium.
column14: The bacterium is inside the cell in a vesicle
column15: The membrane folds inward around the bacterium
column16: The bacterium touches the cell membrane
column17: The membrane pinches off around the bacterium
column28: The bacterium contacts the membrane, the membrane folds in around it, the membrane pinches off, and the bacterium ends up inside a vesicle. This is endocytosis (phagocytosis), and it uses energy, so it is active transport.
column29: Picture a hand closing around a ball: what has to happen before the ball is fully enclosed?
